title: Nakamura Sets New Chess.com Rating Record As Artemiev Pulls Out Last-Second Win
summary: A day after becoming the first 3500-rated Chess.com Blitz player in site history, GM Hikaru Nakamura upped his record to 3503 while streaming Titled Tuesday live from Sithonia, Greece, on October 6. Unfortunately for Nakamura, he did not ultimately win the tournament, an honor which went to GM Vladislav Artemiev after he defeated Nakamura in the final round. Titled Tuesday ft. the highest-rated blitz player ever 🐐 @GMHikaru https://t.co/UYVbs2frlJ In case you missed it, here's this week's broadcast live from Greece: Nakamura had reached exactly 3500 before the event, explaining to Chess.com's Tarjei Svensen, "Unless I'm only going to skip [Titled Tuesday and 3 0 Thursday] every week, there's no way even to keep my rating where it is... I view this as very much a one-time thing and that's also why I made it a big point to go for it yesterday." That's not a typo - Hikaru hits 3500! 👏 https://t.co/ZEJ3EPUCEO "My goal in Titled Tuesday [is] like every Titled Tuesday," he also indicated, meaning victory. "First and foremost, because there are actually people watching [in person], I'd like to be competitive where I'm not losing a bunch of games early. That's the starting point." Nakamura achieved that goal, starting with two self described smooth games, but a draw in the fourth round kept him off the roll of perfect players entering the first break in play. Artemiev was among the 17 who did make 4/4, a list which also included last week's victor GM Wesley So as well as GMs Sina Movahed, Alexey Sarana, Awonder Liang, and Liem Le, among others. As usual, the list of perfect players quickly dwindled exiting the break. Artemiev and So lost to Movahed and Liang in round five, and by the end of round six, just three remained perfect: Le, Sarana, and FM Dincer Tasdogen. A round farther in, that list was down to one. Nakamura contributed by defeating Sarana out of a theoretically drawn opening that Sarana either didn't know or remember, or chose not to pursue.

title: FIDE World Senior Team Championships 2027: Registration opens
summary: FIDE, the German Chess Federation (DSB) and LandesSchachverband Sachsen-Anhalt e. V. invite all FIDE member federations and eligible teams to participate in the World Senior Team Chess Championships taking place in Magdeburg, Germany from March 31 (arrival) to April 11 (departure) 2027. The Championships are open to all players, regardless of rating or title, who reach the required age during the calendar year of the competition. Teams may register only through their national chess federations, and there is no limit on the number of teams per federation. All players on a team must be members of the same national federation. The event will feature four categories: Age 50+ Open, Age 50+ Women, Age 65+ Open, and Age 65+ Women. The Women’s sections will be held subject to a minimum of 10 teams from at least two continents. Registration opens on October 10, 2026, and detailed instructions will be published on the official website. The registration deadline is January 31, 2027. Invitation, schedule, regulations (PDF) Official website: worldseniorteam2027.fide.com Email: worldseniorteam@fide.com

title: "Chess might be one of the least expressive sports I have ever watched"
summary:
When the quiet gets loud

Chess might be one of the least expressive sports I have ever watched. And I don't mean that as a criticism. I come from sport, first as a badminton athlete and now through my work across motorsport. I'm used to being able to see competition.

In badminton, pressure travels through the body. A player gets tighter. A stroke that normally lands doesn't. A "come on!" escapes after an important point. Motorsport gives you almost the opposite extreme: speed, lights, noise, cars fighting for position, drivers taking risks at ridiculous speeds, occasionally making contact while trying to outcalculate each other.

Alpine APL Pipers and FYERS American Gambits | Photo: Global Chess League

Then I watched the Global Chess League. Two people. One board. Almost absolute silence. And the commentators are talking about attack, defence, chaos, sacrifice and control. There is a king being protected, a queen under attack, knights moving into position. Someone is setting something up now that may only make sense several moves later.

Vishwanathan Anand and Javokhir Sindarov on the board | Photo: Global Chess League

I remember watching Javokhir Sindarov opposite Viswanathan Anand. Sindarov's leg kept shaking. Anand sat across from him, arms crossed. At one point, Anand made an unexpected move and immediately glanced up at Sindarov before looking back down. It lasted perhaps a second, but I couldn't stop looking at them.

Was the shaking leg nerves? Completely normal? Did Anand even notice it? When he looked up, was he checking Sindarov's reaction to the move? Was he looking for confirmation that it had worked?

That's when chess became fascinating to me in a completely different way. When everything else is muted, the smallest things become loud. A glance. A leg moving. A pause. Someone leaning back. A smile towards a teammate.

In badminton, I can sometimes tell an athlete is under pressure from the way they're moving before I look at the score. In motorsport, aggression can reveal itself through the way a driver attacks a corner or fights for position. But how do you read pressure when two people are sitting almost completely still? How much are you playing the board, and how much are you playing the person?

The people behind the games

I wasn't new to chess. I'd played casually on chess.com and already learnt, rather painfully, that moving the piece that looks right is not quite a strategy. I've followed ChessBase India, watched Sagar Shah with Samay Raina, and grown up hearing names like Viswanathan Anand, Koneru Humpy and, more recently, Gukesh Dommaraju, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu, Divya Deshmukh and Vidit Gujrathi.

I already respected chess' intelligence. What GCL changed for me was how I watched it. Surprisingly, a huge part of that had very little to do with my ability to understand the board. It was the commentary.

PBG Alaskan Knights and Alpine APL Pipers | Photo: Global Chess League

There were moments when the analysis board completely lost me. A commentator would be five possibilities down a variation while I was still wondering why we couldn't just take the piece sitting there. But then they'd tell me something about the person.

Arjun was creating "chaos" on the board. And then, describing Bibisara Assaubayeva, they said something that stayed with me:

There's no such thing as a position too sharp or an opponent too established for her.

What an interesting way to understand a player. In one line, I suddenly understood how she approaches the game. The commentary wasn’t just helping me understand the board. It was helping me understand the people sitting around it.

Arjun Erigaisi and Nihal Sarin - high stakes on the board! | Photo: Global Chess League

Bibisara Assaubayeva, the expression of the event! | Photo: Global Chess League

And many of those characters weren't actually strangers to me. I knew something of Magnus Carlsen before watching him at GCL. I knew Sagar Shah and Tania Sachdev. I recognised Nihal and Sindarov. I'd encountered these people through YouTube, interviews, clips and chess content long before I sat down to watch the league.

That made me realise something: I think sport sometimes gets backwards. You don't always fall in love with the game first and then discover the people. Sometimes the people are what bring you into the game.

The commentary box | Photo: Global Chess League

ChessBase India, Samay Raina and the wider chess media ecosystem had already done part of the work. GCL simply gave all those stories somewhere to meet. For me, that made the commentary almost as important as the chess itself. Without it, I was watching extraordinary players calculate things I couldn't yet see. With it, I was being invited into their thinking.

A team game, too

It also made the team format far more interesting than I expected. I remember watching Nihal glance towards teammates. Little smiles appeared across tables. Players nodded at one another. Sindarov, Bibisara and the others were still fighting individual battles, but suddenly those battles meant something collectively. And I wanted more of that.

What does a GCL coach tell a team of grandmasters? How much does Nihal's approach change because of what's happening on another board? How do six highly individual players prepare to win together?

Even the familiar "Player of the Match" made me question something. Does a chess league need to borrow the rituals of other sporting leagues? Or, as chess grows as a spectator product, could it create more rituals that are purely its own?

I don't know the answer. It was simply one of those things I found myself thinking about while watching.

Player of the match! | Photo: Global Chess League

Grand, but still close

The setting was beautiful. Bengaluru Palace for the launch ceremony, Lalit Ashok for the matches, the buggies coming in from ITC. The black-and-white details, the lighting, the production, the players. Chess already carries a certain grandeur, and GCL certainly didn't shy away from it.

But despite all of that, it never felt like the sport was being placed further away from the viewer. I've watched sport become increasingly premium, with bigger hospitality, bigger sponsorship packages and bigger experiences, and sometimes accessibility can get lost somewhere along the way. Chess felt different.

The beautiful venue of the Global Chess League | Photo: Global Chess League

The commentators laughed when the digital board initially had its little glitches. Sagar, Tania, Harshit, and the other commentators could move from serious analysis to something completely human within seconds. The people explaining the sport belonged to the same community as the people playing it.

There was expertise and grandeur, but it still felt close to the people watching.

Everyone absolutely engrossed! | Photo: Global Chess League

I kept finding the story in the people

And maybe that is chess' real opportunity. Magnus Carlsen and Ian Nepomniachtchi can sit opposite each other carrying years of history. Nepomniachtchi can eventually beat Carlsen in the GCL final. Nihal can lose a crucial game under time pressure and return the next day to win twice. Sindarov can sit across from some of the greatest players in the sport and look completely at home.

To a chess expert, the story might be in the position. I kept finding the story in the people.

Maybe that's because I'm not a chess expert. Maybe that's exactly the point. I came looking for the emotion I recognise in sport: the noise, movement, aggression and release. Chess gave me all of it. It just made me look much, much closer.

And the trophy goes to... Ganges Grandmasters! | Photo: Global Chess League

About the author

Naganethra Reddy is a former professional badminton athlete from India who now works in sustainability in sport, having worked with Formula E, Extreme E and the World Endurance Championship. She is also a member of Badminton England's Inspire Committee and the Women's Sport Collective Advisory Panel.

Originally from Bengaluru and now based in London, she was inspired to explore chess by her brother - by just how difficult he was to beat! Having spent most of her life around sport, she is interested in what makes people watch, follow and connect with it. She writes about the Global Chess League as a relative newcomer to chess.

title: The oldest chess pieces in the world
summary:
A vital commercial network

The Silk Road is the ancient trade route that connected the cities of the eastern Mediterranean with India and China via Central Asia. It was in fact an entire network of roads along which caravans carried silk, furs, porcelain, works of art, cultural objects and spices westwards through numerous intermediate stops, while gold, silver, precious stones and glass travelled eastwards. Many other goods were transported as well, and at times diseases too, such as the plague in the 14 th century.

Historians regard the period between the 2 nd century BC and the 14 th century AD as the heyday of this trade route. Of course, however, the route had already been used for trade long before that and continued to be used afterwards.

Central Asia during Roman times, with the first Silk Road | Source: Wikimedia Commons

A brief excursion into Uzbek history

The city of Samarkand was an important stopping point along this route. Present-day Samarkand was not built until the 14 th century, close to an older city called Afrasiab. This ancient city had already been founded around 750 BC at an oasis on the Zeravshan River. In the ancient Persian Achaemenid Empire (6 th to 4 th century BC), Afrasiab was the capital of the province of Sogdia. Since the city was favourably situated on the Silk Road and served as a stopping point for merchants, it became very prosperous over time.

The Greeks knew the city as Marakanda, and in 329 BC Alexander the Great conquered this trading centre during his campaigns. In the centuries that followed, Afrasiab came under changing rulers. In AD 712, it was conquered by the Arabs. In 1220, Afrasiab was completely destroyed by the Mongols under Genghis Khan.

In the 14 th century, a new city was built a little further south of the old settlement mound of Afrasiab - Samarkand. The Mongol ruler Timur Lenk made Samarkand the capital of his empire in 1369 and transformed it, with many magnificent buildings, into one of the most important metropolises of its time. Around 150,000 people lived there. Alongside trade and commerce, science and the arts were also promoted.

Depiction of Timur granting audience on the occasion of his accession, in the near contemporary Zafarnama (1424-1428), 1467 edition | Author: Attributed to Bihzād (15 th century), via Wikimedia Commons

In 1500, the Uzbeks, named after their leader Uzbek Khan, conquered Samarkand. After a turbulent history, the Uzbeks, whose settlement areas were divided among various khanates and emirates, became caught up in the conflict of interests between two colonial powers: Russia and Great Britain. The Russian Empire sought to extend its territory southwards, while the British wanted to secure their colonial empire in India to the north. The Russian Empire gained the upper hand in Central Asia and conquered the khanates and emirates or made them dependent. Eventually, Russia established the "Governor-Generalship of Turkestan".

After the Russian Revolution, the Bolsheviks continued the Tsarist colonial policy and expanded Russian-controlled territory in conflicts against the peoples of Central Asia. The Bolsheviks overthrew the local rulers and established republics modelled on the Soviet system, such as the "Khorezm People's Republic" and the "Bukhara People's Republic". In 1925, the Soviet republics of Central Asia were reorganised, and among them the "Uzbek Soviet Socialist Republic (Uzbek SSR)" was created.

The oldest chess pieces in the world

In 1977, archaeologist Yuri Buryakov carried out excavations as part of a major project by the Uzbek Academy of Archaeology in the enormous mound of the destroyed ancient city of Afrasiab near Samarkand. Among other objects, he found seven small ivory figures - a ruler on a chariot, horsemen, an elephant with a soldier and foot soldiers. Since the surfaces of the figures belonging to the set were heavily worn, suggesting that they had often been handled, it seemed likely that the set consisted of chess pieces. This interpretation was also supported by the manner in which the pieces were represented, corresponding to the arrangement found in the Indian game of Chaturanga.

The pieces were found in a layer that also contained, among other things, a coin dating from the year 712, which made it easier to date the figures. The pieces were assigned to the period between the 6 th and 8 th centuries. Since figurative representations were no longer considered appropriate after the spread of Islam in Persia, the pieces must have been made during the late phase of the Sasanian Empire, and therefore no later than the middle of the 7 th century.

The Afrasiab chess pieces are therefore the oldest-known set of chess pieces. They are now kept in the State Museum of Samarkand.

State Museum of Samarkand | Source: Wikimedia Commons

title: The princes of Samarkand
summary:
The following article appeared in the Thüringer Allgemeine on 1 October 2026. Reproduced with kind permission.

The princes of Samarkand

There is a Thuringian story behind Germany's bronze medal at the Chess Olympiad. It is a story of youth development that began two decades ago - and is closely linked to national coach Bernd Vökler from Apolda.

When Rasmus Svane sits down to dinner in Bad Blankenburg a few weeks before the Chess Olympiad, the medal in Samarkand is still a distant dream. The national team players are preparing for the highlight of the season at the regional sports school - supported by grandmaster Peter Svidler, once a second to former world champion Vladimir Kramnik and a commentator for the official YouTube channel at the Olympiad. After a long day of training, Svane jokes that if they manage to win a medal in Uzbekistan, it will surely be thanks to the excellent raspberry spritzer in Bad Blankenburg.

They do. Germany wins bronze - the first medal for a German men's team at a Chess Olympiad in 26 years. The joke about the spritzer becomes a symbol. For many of the paths leading to this success do indeed point to Thuringia.

Above all, they lead to Bernd Vökler. The Apolda native has been Germany's national youth coach since 2003 and has since become one of the most important sources of ideas within the German Chess Federation. Anyone who wants to understand why the current generation is so successful has to look back two decades.

In 2008, the Chess Olympiad is held in Dresden. As the host nation, Germany is allowed to enter three teams - and Vökler uses the opportunity for an experiment. Instead of filling another team with experienced masters, he sends a youth squad into the competition. The young players perform surprisingly well against international opposition.

A year later, Vökler goes a step further. At the time, intensive support in Germany generally begins only at the age of 14 or 15. He wants to start earlier and brings nine- and ten-year-olds into a five-year development programme. The group known as the Chess Princes is born.

Matthias Blübaum, Alexander Donchenko and Rasmus Svane are among them. Seventeen years later, all three are part of Germany's bronze-medal team in Samarkand - together with Vincent Keymer and Frederik Svane, who are six years younger. The Chess Princes of the past have become medal winners.

But early development alone is not enough for Vökler. With the "Chess Year", he gives young elite players the opportunity to spend a year between school and university treating chess as a profession. Blübaum is among the first to try it.

While the national team players are fighting for bronze in Uzbekistan, Vökler is already back in Bad Blankenburg training the next group of young players. When the medal is confirmed, he sends a group photograph of the youngsters to Samarkand. The young princes send their greetings to the crown princes.

Vincent Keymer, Matthias Blübaum, Frederik Svane and Rasmus Svane representing Germany in their round-ten match against France in Samarkand (a 3-1 victory with wins by the Svane brothers on the bottom boards) | Photo: Rafal Oleksiewicz / FIDE

There is also a historical link to Thuringia. When Germany won silver in Istanbul in 2000, its most recent medal until now, grandmaster Thomas Luther was one of the players at the board. Twenty-six years later, he is there again. As head of the relevant FIDE commission, the Erfurt-born grandmaster oversees the Para Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, held alongside the main Olympiad for the first time. At the same time, he watches a new German generation reach the podium - with players, some of whom had not even been born when he helped win silver.

The latest success is likely to have an impact far beyond the sporting result. The Olympiad counts as a so-called target event for German federal funding. Finishing among the world's top three could improve chess' ranking and bring in additional funding of around 120,000 euros per year.

And the next talents are already sitting at the board. Among the most promising is 14-year-old Christian Glöckler. He was discovered and guided to the top by Erfurt grandmaster Thomas Pähtz, who was part of East Germany's Olympiad team in 1988. Vökler, meanwhile, is driving Germany's bid to host the 2028 World Junior Championship in Bad Blankenburg. If the bid succeeds, talents such as Glöckler could be given a major stage in front of a home crowd.

The bronze medal therefore tells a story not only of five grandmasters and two remarkable weeks in Uzbekistan. It also tells of decisions taken when some of these players were still children. And of youth development whose rewards in chess often become visible only several moves later.

Many people played a part in the success in Samarkand. But an important part of its story begins in Thuringia - with Bernd Vökler's bold idea. And, Rasmus Svane might add, a little with the raspberry spritzer from Bad Blankenburg.

title: German chess magazine SCHACH launches first English edition as CHESS INSIGHT
summary:
A 180-year publishing tradition enters a new chapter

Including its predecessor magazines, SCHACH’s publishing tradition stretches back around 180 years. The magazine is known for in-depth tournament coverage, extensively annotated games, interviews, background stories and contributions from leading players, coaches and chess journalists.

Chess has always crossed borders. Players from different countries, cultures and generations meet over the same 64 squares and share a language that needs no translation. With this English edition, we want our journalism, analysis and stories to cross another border as well.

CHESS INSIGHT aims to offer more than tournament results and moves. Its focus is on the stories behind the games: what happened behind the scenes, what players were thinking at critical moments and what readers can learn from their decisions.

CHESS INSIGHT 01/2026

The first issue contains 84 pages and is available from Forward Chess for US$2.99:

CHESS INSIGHT 01/2026 on Forward Chess

It covers major recent events including the Grand Chess Tour and Sinquefield Cup in St. Louis, the Sparkassen Chess Meeting Dortmund and the Esports World Cup in Paris.

A particular highlight is an extensive feature with Peter Leko, coach of German grandmaster Vincent Keymer, offering insights from the perspective of a world-class player and trainer.

The issue also includes the regular SCHACH Questions feature with photographer Lennart Ootes, as well as training material, combinations, problems and studies, reviews and chess history.

Among the contributors to the issue are Peter Leko, Dr. Karsten Müller, Elisabeth Pähtz and Dmitrij Kollars.

Interactive reading with Forward Chess

On Forward Chess, games and analyses can be followed directly on an interactive chessboard. Readers can play through variations and examine positions move by move while reading the accompanying text — an ideal format for the deeply annotated games that are one of SCHACH’s traditional strengths.

With CHESS INSIGHT, one of Germany’s longest-standing chess publishing traditions is now opening itself to an international readership.

Contact and cooperation

If you are interested in subscribing to CHESS INSIGHT, distributing the magazine or exploring a cooperation or partnership, please contact our Editor-in-Chief:

IM Jonathan Carlstedt

title: Vlastimil Hort Tournament 2026: Return to Hotel Don Giovanni
summary:
Last year, we launched a tournament that was intended to be much more than just another rapid event on the chess calendar. Vlastimil Hort is a true legend for several generations of Czech chess players, and Don Giovanni is the perfect place for us all to come together in his honour!

Tournament director Petr Boleslav

Hotel Don Giovanni was not chosen as the venue by chance. It was here that Vlastimil Hort regularly stayed during his visits to Prague. The hotel therefore became one of the places closely associated with the later years of his life and his returns to the Czech capital.

Our hotels became a second home for Vlastimil Hort whenever he returned to Prague. We had the honour of knowing him not only as a chess legend, but above all as a wonderful person and a dear friend. I am delighted that we have established a tradition that will carry his name forward and commemorate, year after year, a remarkable man who will not be forgotten!

Jaroslav Svoboda, owner of CZECH INN HOTELS, the hotel group to which Don Giovanni belongs

The Vlastimil Hort Suite in the Hotel Don Giovanni | Photo: Nils Rohde

Vlastimil Hort was one of the finest Czechoslovak chess players. For many years, he ranked among the world’s leading players, represented Czechoslovakia and later the Czech Republic, and became a prominent figure who had a remarkable ability to bring chess closer to the wider public. Above all, the Vlastimil Hort Tournament is intended as a celebration of chess and of a man who represented the game at home and around the world for decades.

Seven Rounds of Rapid Chess

This year’s tournament will take place on Saturday, 21 November 2026 at Hotel Don Giovanni Prague. It will be played over seven rounds using the Swiss system, with a time control of 15 minutes per player plus a 10-second increment for each move. The tournament will be FIDE/Elo-rated.

Player registration will take place from 8.00am to 8.45am. At 9.00am, the wife of the legendary grandmaster, Mrs Brigitte Hort, will officially open the tournament in person with an introductory address. The first three rounds will be followed by a one-hour break, with the remaining four rounds beginning at 1.00pm. The closing ceremony and prize-giving are scheduled for 5.15pm, when Mrs Hort, together with the organisers, will present the awards to the leading players.

Jaroslav Svoboda, Brigitte Hort and Petr Boleslav | Photo: Organiser

More than CZK 15,000 in Prizes

In 2026, the leading players can look forward to a significantly larger prize fund. The tournament winner will receive CZK 4,000, the runner-up CZK 3,000 and the third-placed player CZK 2,000, with cash prizes also awarded for further places.

Separate prizes of CZK 500 will be awarded to the best senior player aged 65+, the best female player and the best junior player under the age of 15. Books by Grandmaster Vlastimil Hort will once again form part of the tournament’s traditional non-cash prizes.

Mrs Brigitte Hort is once again making a personal financial contribution to this year’s prize fund. She will also donate an item from Vlastimil Hort’s collection as a special prize.

Vlastimil Hort Tournament 2026

Saturday, 21 November 2026

Hotel Don Giovanni Prague, Vinohradská 157a, Prague 3 – Žižkov

The entry fee is CZK 200 , payable on site during registration. Players may register in advance by email at petr.boleslav@gmail.com no later than 18 November 2026 .

Special accommodation rates are also available for tournament participants.

The tournament is organised by Czech Inn Chess .
